Plug-In Tail Estimation

Overview¶

Plug-in tail estimation fits a tail model and evaluates a quantity of interest under that fitted model. If a distribution family is indexed by a parameter θ\thetaθ and the target functional is T(θ)T(\theta)T(θ), its plug-in estimate is T(θ^)T(\widehat\theta)T(θ). The parameter can include a tail exponent, scale, and tail probability; an exponent alone generally does not determine the target.

For an exact Pareto distribution, estimating the exponent from logarithms can give more concentrated mean estimates than the sample mean. This page establishes a comparison of asymptotic error scales and explains how finite-sample error comparisons must handle non-finite fits. It does not claim uniformly smaller mean squared error (MSE). The unregularized plug-in mean has its own singularity at the mean-existence boundary.

A regularly varying tail only specifies limiting tail ratios. Using a Hill estimate in a functional requires a threshold choice, a tail approximation, and any body contribution to that functional. The exact model below isolates the estimation mechanism before these modeling uncertainties enter.

Here α\alphaα is the tail exponent, xmx_mxm​ is the lower cutoff, and the extreme-value index is ξ=1/α\xi=1/\alphaξ=1/α. We write μ=E[X]\mu=\mathbb E[X]μ=E[X] and Xˉn=n−1∑i=1nXi\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_iXˉn​=n−1∑i=1n​Xi​ for the population and sample means.

Exact Pareto mean with a known cutoff¶

Assume X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ are independent and identically distributed (iid), with

P(Xi>x)=(xmx)α,x≥xm>0,\begin{gathered} \mathbb P(X_i>x)=\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha,\\ x\ge x_m>0, \end{gathered}P(Xi​>x)=(xxm​​)α,x≥xm​>0,​
(1)

where xmx_mxm​ is known and fixed, and the true exponent satisfies α>1\alpha>1α>1. These are assumptions about the entire distribution. The Pareto moment formula gives

μ=αxmα−1=xm1−ξ.\mu=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1}=\frac{x_m}{1-\xi}.μ=α−1αxm​​=1−ξxm​​.
(2)

The maximum-likelihood estimate of the exponent and its reciprocal are

ξ^n=1n∑i=1nlog⁡(Xi/xm),α^n=1ξ^n.\begin{gathered} \widehat\xi_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_i/x_m),\\ \widehat\alpha_n=\frac1{\widehat\xi_n}. \end{gathered}ξ​n​=n1​i=1∑n​log(Xi​/xm​),αn​=ξ​n​1​.​
(3)

They use all observations above a known cutoff. Hill instead averages the top kkk log-excesses above the random order-statistic threshold Xn−k:nX_{n-k:n}Xn−k:n​. The formulas share a log-excess mechanism, but their sample sizes and threshold assumptions differ.

The plug-in mean is

μ^n=xm1−ξ^n=α^nxmα^n−1,ξ^n<1.\begin{gathered} \begin{aligned} \widehat\mu_n&=\frac{x_m}{1-\widehat\xi_n}\\ &=\frac{\widehat\alpha_n x_m}{\widehat\alpha_n-1}, \end{aligned}\\ \widehat\xi_n<1. \end{gathered}μ​n​​=1−ξ​n​xm​​=αn​−1αn​xm​​,​ξ​n​<1.​
(4)

Use pareto_mean_plugin.

from xmath.incerto.estimators import pareto_mean_plugin

for sample in ([1, 1], [1, 2], [4, 4]):
    print(f"{sample} {pareto_mean_plugin(sample, x_m=1):.4g}")

Output

[1, 1] 1
[1, 2] 1.53
[4, 4] inf

An all-cutoff sample uses the limiting mean xmx_mxm​; a fit with ξ^n≥1\widehat\xi_n\ge1ξ​n​≥1 has no finite mean.

Why the logarithmic fit can improve concentration¶

For each fixed α>1\alpha>1α>1, the finite plug-in estimates have the asymptotic law

L ⁣(n(μ^n−μ)∣ξ^n<1)⇒N ⁣(0,xm2α2(α−1)4),n→∞.\begin{gathered} \mathcal L\!\left(\sqrt n(\widehat\mu_n-\mu) \mid \widehat\xi_n<1\right)\\ \Rightarrow\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{x_m^2\alpha^2}{(\alpha-1)^4}\right),\\ n\to\infty. \end{gathered}L(n​(μ​n​−μ)∣ξ​n​<1)⇒N(0,(α−1)4xm2​α2​),n→∞.​
(5)

Here L(⋅∣⋅)\mathcal L(\cdot\mid\cdot)L(⋅∣⋅) denotes a conditional sampling law, ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ denotes convergence in distribution, and N(0,v)\mathcal N(0,v)N(0,v) is the centered normal law with variance vvv. The probability of a non-finite fit tends to zero. Thus central error quantiles shrink on the n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 scale. This is a distributional claim; the variance in the normal limit is not a claim about the finite-sample variance of μ^n\widehat\mu_nμ​n​.

For 1<α<21<\alpha<21<α<2, the sample mean remains consistent, but its error scale is n1/α−1n^{1/\alpha-1}n1/α−1. More precisely, the generalized central limit theorem gives a nondegenerate, non-Gaussian α\alphaα-stable limit for n1−1/α(Xˉn−μ)n^{1-1/\alpha}(\bar X_n-\mu)n1−1/α(Xˉn​−μ) in this exact Pareto model Resnick (2007). That scale decays more slowly than n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2. Large observations can continue to move sample means in this regime; pre-asymptotic LLN behavior illustrates this effect.

Derivation of the Pareto fit and its normal limit¶

We derive the known-cutoff fit and the displayed plug-in limit using the ordinary iid central limit theorem and the delta method. The general limit theorems are cited from van der Vaart 1998, Chapters 2–3; the stable limit for the sample mean is cited above.

Proposition 1 (Known-cutoff Pareto fit and finite-fit normal limit)

Let X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\ldotsX1​,X2​,… be iid exact Pareto Type I variables with known cutoff xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and true exponent α>1\alpha>1α>1. Put ξ=1/α\xi=1/\alphaξ=1/α, μ=αxm/(α−1)\mu=\alpha x_m/(\alpha-1)μ=αxm​/(α−1), and ξ^n=n−1∑i=1nlog⁡(Xi/xm)\widehat\xi_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_i/x_m)ξ​n​=n−1∑i=1n​log(Xi​/xm​). Whenever the log-excess sum is positive, the unique likelihood maximizer over exponents in (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) is α^n=1/ξ^n\widehat\alpha_n=1/\widehat\xi_nαn​=1/ξ​n​. If all observations equal xmx_mxm​, there is no finite maximizer; use the limiting mean xmx_mxm​ as the plug-in convention. Define μ^n=xm/(1−ξ^n)\widehat\mu_n=x_m/(1-\widehat\xi_n)μ​n​=xm​/(1−ξ​n​) for ξ^n<1\widehat\xi_n<1ξ​n​<1, and μ^n=∞\widehat\mu_n=\inftyμ​n​=∞ otherwise. Then P(ξ^n<1)→1P(\widehat\xi_n<1)\to1P(ξ​n​<1)→1 and

L ⁣(n(μ^n−μ)∣ξ^n<1)⇒N ⁣(0,xm2α2(α−1)4).\mathcal L\!\left(\sqrt n(\widehat\mu_n-\mu) \mid\widehat\xi_n<1\right) \Rightarrow\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{x_m^2\alpha^2}{(\alpha-1)^4}\right).L(n​(μ​n​−μ)∣ξ​n​<1)⇒N(0,(α−1)4xm2​α2​).
(6)
Proof 1

Set Yi=log⁡(Xi/xm)Y_i=\log(X_i/x_m)Yi​=log(Xi​/xm​). For y≥0y\ge0y≥0,

P(Yi>y)=P(Xi>xmey)=e−αy.\begin{aligned} \mathbb P(Y_i>y)&=\mathbb P(X_i>x_m e^y)\\ &=e^{-\alpha y}. \end{aligned}P(Yi​>y)​=P(Xi​>xm​ey)=e−αy.​
(7)

Thus YiY_iYi​ is exponential with mean 1/α1/\alpha1/α and variance 1/α21/\alpha^21/α2, even when XiX_iXi​ has infinite variance. Up to terms independent of α\alphaα, the log likelihood is nlog⁡α−α∑iYin\log\alpha-\alpha\sum_iY_inlogα−α∑i​Yi​. Its derivative vanishes at α^n=n/∑iYi\widehat\alpha_n=n/\sum_iY_iαn​=n/∑i​Yi​, and its second derivative is −n/α2<0-n/\alpha^2<0−n/α2<0. This proves the fit formula when ∑iYi>0\sum_iY_i>0∑i​Yi​>0, an event of probability one under the continuous model. If the sum is zero, the log likelihood is nlog⁡αn\log\alphanlogα plus a constant and increases without bound; the fitted mean tends to xmx_mxm​ as α→∞\alpha\to\inftyα→∞.

The law of large numbers gives ξ^n→1/α<1\widehat\xi_n\to1/\alpha<1ξ​n​→1/α<1 almost surely. The central limit theorem gives

n(ξ^n−ξ)⇒N(0,ξ2).\sqrt n(\widehat\xi_n-\xi) \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\xi^2).n​(ξ​n​−ξ)⇒N(0,ξ2).
(8)

For the locally smooth function h(t)=xm/(1−t)h(t)=x_m/(1-t)h(t)=xm​/(1−t), h′(ξ)=xm/(1−ξ)2h'(\xi)=x_m/(1-\xi)^2h′(ξ)=xm​/(1−ξ)2. The delta method therefore gives limiting variance

[h′(ξ)]2ξ2=xm2ξ2(1−ξ)4=xm2α2(α−1)4.\begin{aligned} [h'(\xi)]^2\xi^2&=\frac{x_m^2\xi^2}{(1-\xi)^4}\\ &=\frac{x_m^2\alpha^2}{(\alpha-1)^4}. \end{aligned}[h′(ξ)]2ξ2​=(1−ξ)4xm2​ξ2​=(α−1)4xm2​α2​.​
(9)

Because P(ξ^n<1)→1\mathbb P(\widehat\xi_n<1)\to1P(ξ​n​<1)→1, conditioning on finite fits does not change this weak limit. Formally, apply the delta method to a smooth extension of hhh from a neighborhood of ξ<1\xi<1ξ<1; with probability tending to one it agrees with the finite-fit formula.

The gain comes from averaging exponential log-excesses and using the assumed Pareto shape to extrapolate the mean. It depends on that shape being correct.

Error-scale comparison¶

At α=1.5\alpha=1.5α=1.5 and xm=1x_m=1xm​=1, μ=3\mu=3μ=3 and the normal-limit variance coefficient for the plug-in mean is 36. Its central absolute error scale is therefore 6/n6/\sqrt n6/n​, or 2/n2/\sqrt n2/n​ relative to μ\muμ. The sample mean’s stable-limit scale is proportional to n−1/3n^{-1/3}n−1/3. The unknown comparison constants and finite-sample behavior are not supplied by comparing these powers of nnn.

In a repeated-sample experiment with a finite true mean, non-finite fits count as infinite errors. Removing them changes the sampling law. Below we report fit frequencies, not an unconditional MSE or a finite-only error comparison.

The singularity and the frequency of infinite fits¶

Proposition 2 (Exact probability of an infinite Pareto mean fit)

For n≥1n\ge1n≥1 iid exact Pareto observations with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and true α>0\alpha>0α>0, set ξ^n=n−1∑ilog⁡(Xi/xm)\widehat\xi_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\log(X_i/x_m)ξ​n​=n−1∑i​log(Xi​/xm​) and use the finite-fit convention μ^n=xm/(1−ξ^n)\widehat\mu_n=x_m/(1-\widehat\xi_n)μ​n​=xm​/(1−ξ​n​) when ξ^n<1\widehat\xi_n<1ξ​n​<1, and infinity otherwise. Then nξ^n∼Gamma(n,rate α)n\widehat\xi_n\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(n,\text{rate }\alpha)nξ​n​∼Gamma(n,rate α) and

P(μ^n=∞)=P(ξ^n≥1).P(\widehat\mu_n=\infty)=P(\widehat\xi_n\ge1).P(μ​n​=∞)=P(ξ​n​≥1).
(10)

This probability is strictly between zero and one for every finite nnn. When α=1\alpha=1α=1, it tends to 1/21/21/2 as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞.

Proof 2

The log-excesses are iid exponential with rate α\alphaα for every α>0\alpha>0α>0. The Gamma law follows by multiplying the exponential MGFs (α/(α−t))n(\alpha/(\alpha-t))^n(α/(α−t))n for t<αt<\alphat<α; the boundary event has probability zero. The gamma density is positive on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), so both fit events have positive probability. At the boundary α=1\alpha=1α=1, the ordinary CLT for the log-excesses gives an infinite-fit probability tending to 1/21/21/2.

This is the exact probability used in the figure. A finite estimate can occur even when the true mean is infinite.

Use pareto_plugin_nonfinite_probability.

from xmath.incerto.limits import pareto_plugin_nonfinite_probability

for alpha in (.8, 1, 1.5):
    p = pareto_plugin_nonfinite_probability(alpha, 30)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:g}: finite={1-p:.4g}, infinite={p:.4g}")

Output

alpha=0.8: finite=0.1321, infinite=0.8679
alpha=1: finite=0.5243, infinite=0.4757
alpha=1.5: finite=0.9927, infinite=0.007337

Regenerate with uv run python demos/incerto/visualization_p2.py.

Neither the normal limit nor a finite simulation establishes MSE dominance or tests whether an empirical dataset is Pareto.

When only the tail is modeled¶

Proposition 3 (Mean decomposition with an exact Pareto conditional tail)

Let X≥0X\ge0X≥0 have CDF FFF and fix a threshold u>0u>0u>0 with tail probability Fˉ(u)=P(X>u)>0\bar F(u)=\mathbb P(X>u)>0Fˉ(u)=P(X>u)>0. Suppose the conditional tail is exactly Pareto:

P(X>x∣X>u)=(u/x)α,x≥u,α>1.\begin{gathered} \mathbb P(X>x\mid X>u)=(u/x)^\alpha,\\ x\ge u,\quad \alpha>1. \end{gathered}P(X>x∣X>u)=(u/x)α,x≥u,α>1.​
(11)

Then the finite mean μ=EX\mu=\mathbb E Xμ=EX is

μ=E[X1{X≤u}]+Fˉ(u)uαα−1.\begin{aligned} \mu&=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X\le u\}}]\\ &\quad+\bar F(u)\frac{u\alpha}{\alpha-1}. \end{aligned}μ​=E[X1{X≤u}​]+Fˉ(u)α−1uα​.​
(12)
Proof 3

The mean-excess formula gives E[X∣X>u]=u+e(u)=uα/(α−1)\mathbb E[X\mid X>u]=u+e(u)=u\alpha/(\alpha-1)E[X∣X>u]=u+e(u)=uα/(α−1), where e(u)=E[X−u∣X>u]e(u)=\mathbb E[X-u\mid X>u]e(u)=E[X−u∣X>u]. Splitting the expectation at uuu yields the displayed identity. The body term is bounded by uuu and the tail term is finite because α>1\alpha>1α>1.

For an iid sample, let k=∑i1{Xi>u}k=\sum_i\mathbf1_{\{X_i>u\}}k=∑i​1{Xi​>u}​ be the exceedance count. Estimate Fˉ(u)\bar F(u)Fˉ(u) by k/nk/nk/n and fit α^u\widehat\alpha_uαu​ from those exceedances. When k>0k>0k>0 and α^u>1\widehat\alpha_u>1αu​>1, a body-plus-tail estimate is

μ^u=1n∑i=1nXi1{Xi≤u}+knuα^uα^u−1.\begin{aligned} \widehat\mu_u&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\mathbf1_{\{X_i\le u\}}\\ &\quad+\frac{k}{n}\frac{u\widehat\alpha_u}{\widehat\alpha_u-1}. \end{aligned}μ​u​​=n1​i=1∑n​Xi​1{Xi​≤u}​+nk​αu​−1uαu​​.​
(13)

The first term is the body’s contribution per original observation, not the mean conditional on being in the body. The second includes the threshold itself as well as the mean excess. With no exceedances there is no fitted tail exponent; a missing tail fit should be reported. If the fitted exponent is at most 1, the fitted conditional mean is infinite.

A mixture calculation shows why both contributions are needed.

Consider a uniform body on [1,3][1,3][1,3] with probability 0.8, and a Pareto tail with cutoff u=3u=3u=3 and exponent α=1.5\alpha=1.5α=1.5 with probability 0.2. The body conditional mean is 2, the tail conditional mean is 9, and

E[X]=0.8⋅2+0.2⋅9=3.4.\mathbb E[X]=0.8\cdot2+0.2\cdot9=3.4.E[X]=0.8⋅2+0.2⋅9=3.4.
(14)

Using 9 as the whole-distribution mean would omit the body and tail mass. Fitting every observation as exact Pareto from 1 would also impose the wrong model. This is a population calculation, not a simulated estimator ranking.

For empirical thresholds, repeat the analysis over plausible uuu or kkk. Regular variation supports a Pareto approximation far into the tail, not an exact conditional model at a chosen finite threshold. The known-cutoff n\sqrt nn​ calculation does not supply a rate or confidence interval for a Hill fit with a selected threshold.

A missing contribution requires a tail model¶

The hidden-tail result gives the unconditional contribution T1(u)=E[X1{X>u}]T_1(u)=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}]T1​(u)=E[X1{X>u}​], for an exact Pareto parent and α>1\alpha>1α>1:

T1(u)=αxmα−1(xmu)α−1,u≥xm.\begin{gathered} T_1(u)=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1} \left(\frac{x_m}{u}\right)^{\alpha-1},\\ u\ge x_m. \end{gathered}T1​(u)=α−1αxm​​(uxm​​)α−1,u≥xm​.​
(15)

Replacing α\alphaα by an estimate turns this into a model-based tail contribution. It does not make the true population’s unobserved tail empirical. With a tail-only model, its fitted mass and body contribution must also be included, as in the preceding decomposition.

Proposition 4 (Adding the model tail beyond the sample maximum biases the mean upward)

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be iid exact Pareto observations with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, α>1\alpha>1α>1, and n≥1n\ge1n≥1. Set Mn=max⁡iXiM_n=\max_iX_iMn​=maxi​Xi​ and Xˉn=n−1∑iXi\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_iXˉn​=n−1∑i​Xi​. For an independent draw XXX from that law, let T1(u)=E[X1{X>u}]T_1(u)=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}]T1​(u)=E[X1{X>u}​]. Then E[Xˉn+T1(Mn)]>EX\mathbb E[\bar X_n+T_1(M_n)]>\mathbb E XE[Xˉn​+T1​(Mn​)]>EX, with both expectations finite.

Proof 4

The sample mean is unbiased. The displayed Pareto tail formula gives 0<T1(Mn)≤EX<∞0<T_1(M_n)\le\mathbb E X<\infty0<T1​(Mn​)≤EX<∞ almost surely, so the added term has a strictly positive finite expectation.

Debiasing, conditional selection, and clipping¶

The inverse-gamma law provides exact calibration for a known Pareto cutoff.

Proposition 5 (Conditional selection and clipping of a corrected Pareto exponent)

For an integer m>1m>1m>1, take iid exact Pareto observations with known xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>0\alpha>0α>0, and define the corrected estimate α^=(m−1)/∑i=1mlog⁡(Xi/xm)\widehat\alpha=(m-1)/\sum_{i=1}^m\log(X_i/x_m)α=(m−1)/∑i=1m​log(Xi​/xm​), whose denominator is positive almost surely. Fix h>1h>1h>1. The estimate is unbiased and has inverse-gamma density fα^f_{\widehat\alpha}fα​ with shape mmm and scale (m−1)α(m-1)\alpha(m−1)α. Conditional on α^>h\widehat\alpha>hα>h, its density is fα^(a)/P(α^>h)f_{\widehat\alpha}(a)/P(\widehat\alpha>h)fα​(a)/P(α>h) for a>ha>ha>h. Clipping to max⁡(α^,h)\max(\widehat\alpha,h)max(α,h) instead gives an atom P(α^≤h)P(\widehat\alpha\le h)P(α≤h) at hhh and density fα^f_{\widehat\alpha}fα​ above hhh. The corresponding plug-in mean, obtained by applying a↦xma/(a−1)a\mapsto x_ma/(a-1)a↦xm​a/(a−1) to the selected or clipped exponent, is at most xmh/(h−1)x_mh/(h-1)xm​h/(h−1) in either case; clipping attains the bound at its atom.

Proof 5

The corrected estimate is (m−1)/m(m-1)/m(m−1)/m times the known-cutoff maximum-likelihood estimate m/∑ilog⁡(Xi/xm)m/\sum_i\log(X_i/x_m)m/∑i​log(Xi​/xm​). The cited inverse-gamma law gives shape mmm and scale (m−1)α(m-1)\alpha(m−1)α after this rescaling. Conditional on α^>h\widehat\alpha>hα>h, the density is

fα^(a)P(α^>h),a>h.\frac{f_{\widehat\alpha}(a)}{P(\widehat\alpha>h)},\qquad a>h.P(α>h)fα​(a)​,a>h.
(16)

The cited inverse-gamma mean is (m−1)α/(m−1)=α(m-1)\alpha/(m-1)=\alpha(m−1)α/(m−1)=α. Clipping α^\widehat\alphaα to max⁡(α^,h)\max(\widehat\alpha,h)max(α,h) instead gives an atom of size P(α^≤h)P(\widehat\alpha\le h)P(α≤h) at hhh and retains the unconditional density above it. The function a↦xma/(a−1)a\mapsto x_ma/(a-1)a↦xm​a/(a−1) is decreasing on a>1a>1a>1, giving the bound and its attainment at hhh.

The conditional law differs from the corrected estimator’s unconditional sampling law. Either choice changes the estimator or the samples being reported. Neither operation preserves unbiasedness or establishes mean-squared-error superiority.

Use pareto_exponent_sampling to expose the selection mass instead of silently omitting estimates. The h=1h=1h=1 row reports that mass at the mean boundary, where the finite upper bound above does not apply.

from xmath.incerto.extremes import pareto_exponent_sampling

law = pareto_exponent_sampling(1.2, 20, debiased=True)
for h in (1, 1.1, 1.3):
    print(f"h={h:g}: retained={law.sf(h):.4g}, excluded or clipped={law.cdf(h):.4g}")

Output

h=1: retained=0.7495, excluded or clipped=0.2505
h=1.1: retained=0.5929, excluded or clipped=0.4071
h=1.3: retained=0.3088, excluded or clipped=0.6912

Appendix E, pp. 189–191, especially E.1, is the SCoFT v4 source context Taleb, 2025. Its finite-sample calibration must be restricted to an exact Pareto model, with known cutoff or the fixed-kkk Hill experiment. A general slowly varying factor need not be constant. The singularity proof below rules out finite unconditional MSE for the unregularized plug-in mean, even when central error quantiles look small.

Caveats¶

The moment boundary is also an estimation boundary.

Proposition 6 (Sensitivity of the Pareto mean to its exponent)

For fixed xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>1\alpha>1α>1, the exact Pareto mean μ(α)=αxm/(α−1)\mu(\alpha)=\alpha x_m/(\alpha-1)μ(α)=αxm​/(α−1) satisfies

dμdα=−xm(α−1)2.\frac{d\mu}{d\alpha}=-\frac{x_m}{(\alpha-1)^2}.dαdμ​=−(α−1)2xm​​.
(17)
Proof 6

Differentiate μ(α)=xm+xm/(α−1)\mu(\alpha)=x_m+x_m/(\alpha-1)μ(α)=xm​+xm​/(α−1).

Small exponent errors can therefore produce large mean errors near α=1\alpha=1α=1. An uncertainty interval for α\alphaα that reaches 1 cannot be mapped to a finite upper bound for this Pareto mean. The fixed-α\alphaα normal approximation above is not uniform as α↓1\alpha\downarrow1α↓1.

There is a stronger finite-sample warning.

Proposition 7 (Infinite moments of the unregularized finite-fit mean)

Let n≥1n\ge1n≥1 observations be iid exact Pareto with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and any α>0\alpha>0α>0. Set ξ^n=n−1∑ilog⁡(Xi/xm)\widehat\xi_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\log(X_i/x_m)ξ​n​=n−1∑i​log(Xi​/xm​), and μ^n=xm/(1−ξ^n)\widehat\mu_n=x_m/(1-\widehat\xi_n)μ​n​=xm​/(1−ξ​n​) on ξ^n<1\widehat\xi_n<1ξ​n​<1, with infinity otherwise. For r=1,2r=1,2r=1,2,

E[μ^nr∣ξ^n<1]=∞.\mathbb E[\widehat\mu_n^r\mid\widehat\xi_n<1]=\infty.E[μ​nr​∣ξ​n​<1]=∞.
(18)

Also P(μ^n=∞)>0P(\widehat\mu_n=\infty)>0P(μ​n​=∞)>0 at every finite nnn.

Proof 7

By Proposition 2, ξ^n\widehat\xi_nξ​n​ has a gamma density fn(t)=(nα)ntn−1e−nαt/Γ(n)f_n(t)=(n\alpha)^n t^{n-1}e^{-n\alpha t}/\Gamma(n)fn​(t)=(nα)ntn−1e−nαt/Γ(n) for t>0t>0t>0, obtained by averaging nnn independent exponential log-excesses. Here Γ\GammaΓ is the gamma function. The density is continuous and strictly positive at t=1t=1t=1. For any sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, the first-moment integral includes

∫1−ε1xm1−tfn(t) dt=∞;\int_{1-\varepsilon}^1\frac{x_m}{1-t}f_n(t)\,dt=\infty;∫1−ε1​1−txm​​fn​(t)dt=∞;
(19)

replacing xm/(1−t)x_m/(1-t)xm​/(1−t) by its square gives a divergent second-moment integral. Conditioning on t<1t<1t<1 only divides these integrals by a positive probability. Moreover, P(ξ^n≥1)>0\mathbb P(\widehat\xi_n \ge1)>0P(ξ​n​≥1)>0 for every finite nnn.

Finite simulations can easily miss the singularity. Clipping or constraining the exponent away from 1 changes the estimator and must be disclosed, with its bias and any risk claim assessed separately.

Model uncertainty remains after sampling error shrinks. A fitted exponent does not determine the scale, tail probability, or body of the distribution. Truncation, dependence, measurement limits, or an incorrectly chosen threshold can invalidate the exact-model calibration. Report those assumptions alongside threshold sensitivity and uncertainty propagated through the functional. If the true exact Pareto exponent is at most 1, there is no finite population mean to recover by this method.
